item.title: Spin quantum computing
item.description: Qubits from single electron and hole spins in semiconductor quantum dots, and how to make them scale.

item.title: Light–matter interaction

item.title: Open quantum systems
item.description: Quantum systems that exchange energy and particles with their environment, and how to turn this into a tool.

item.title: Topological matter
item.description: Protected edge states, Majorana modes and quantum geometry in driven and nanoscale systems.

item.title: A new website
item.description:
The website got a makeover: faster, phone-friendly, and now with a dark mode for late-night reading of papers.

There is also a spin on the home page that will happily precess for you. Unlike the ones in the lab, it never decoheres.

item.title: Floquet physics from quantized light-matter interaction: geometric phases, gauge consistency, and entanglement
item.description: How Floquet physics of classically driven systems emerges from fully quantized light-matter interaction.

item.title: Modeling of flopping-mode spin qubits: Beyond the two-site model
item.description: A spatially resolved model of flopping-mode spin qubits that goes beyond the usual two-site description.

item.title: Multi-cavity strong coupling to an electron spin ensemble: spectral and dark-state signatures
item.description: Several superconducting cavities strongly coupled to one spin ensemble, with signatures of dark states.

item.title: Lindblad theory of linear response susceptibility and dispersive readout in minimal Kitaev junctions
item.description: A Lindblad-based linear response theory for readout of hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots.

item.title: Public talk: when spins learn to compute
item.description:
I gave a public talk in the series Faszination Mathematik und Physik of the University of Augsburg, in the Zeughaus Augsburg: Wenn Spins rechnen lernen – Auf dem Weg zu skalierbaren Quantencomputern (when spins learn to compute: on the way to scalable quantum computers).

Quantum computers promise computing power beyond today’s computers, but for that single qubits have to get better and millions of them have to work together. Since all classical computers are built on semiconductor chips, it makes sense to build quantum computers from semiconductors too, with qubits made from the spin of single electrons. The talk followed these spins as they learn to compute, one trick at a time.

item.title: Humboldt Research Fellowship for Beatriz Pérez González
item.description:
Congratulations to Beatriz Pérez González, who has won a Humboldt Research Fellowship from the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation! Beatriz joined our group in 2024, and since March 2026 she continues her research here as a Humboldt fellow.

She studies what happens when light and matter interact strongly in semiconductor spin qubits, and how microwave photons could link qubits that sit far apart on a chip. Her theoretical models look for realistic devices in which this regime can be reached and put to use.

item.title: Fast coherent control of a charge qubit on solid neon with a spin-qubit-compatible resonator
item.description: A charge qubit on solid neon with fast coherent control, coupled to a magnetic-field-compatible resonator.

item.title: Keynote at the Virtual Engine Conference 2026
item.description:
I gave one of the opening keynotes at the 5th Virtual Engine Conference of the DLR Institute of Test and Simulation for Gas Turbines in Augsburg: Modelling and simulation of scalable quantum computers.

Over 70 participants from science and industry, from gas turbines to AI-driven engineering, met to discuss the latest digital developments. A nice chance to show how quantum computers are designed on the computer before they are built, and what they might one day compute for engineering.

item.title: NbTiN nanowire resonators and prospects for spin-photon coupling with electrons on solid neon
item.description: Superconducting NbTiN nanowire resonators keep their high quality on solid neon, a step toward spin qubits with electrons on neon.

item.title: Escaping AB caging via Floquet engineering: photo-induced long-range interference in an all-band-flat model
item.description: Periodic driving lets particles escape Aharonov-Bohm caging in a flat-band diamond chain.

item.title: Electrical readout of spins in the absence of spin blockade
item.description: A way to read out spins electrically even when spin blockade is lifted.

item.title: Readout of multi-level quantum geometry from electronic transport
item.description: A protocol to measure the quantum geometric tensor in tunnel and molecular junctions.

item.title: Polarimetry with Spins in the Solid State
item.description: Pauli spin blockade, the standard spin readout in semiconductor qubits, seen as polarimetry with spins.

item.title: SymPT: a comprehensive tool for automating effective Hamiltonian derivations
item.description: SymPT, a software tool that automates Schrieffer-Wolff transformations for effective Hamiltonians.

item.title: Closed-Form Generators for Perturbative Transformations in Static and Periodically Driven Quantum Systems
item.description: A closed-form expression for the generator of perturbative transformations, for static and periodically driven systems.

item.title: Unified linear response theory of quantum electronic circuits
item.description: One theory for the electrical response of quantum devices at any frequency, including relaxation and dephasing.

item.title: New European project GeMOS: germanium MOSFETs for quantum computation
item.description:
Our group is now part of GeMOS, a QuantERA project funded through the DFG in Germany, together with teams in Bratislava (coordinator Peter Stano), Regensburg, Basel and ETH Zurich.

The project studies holes in germanium metal-oxide-semiconductor nanostructures, a material platform that has not been used for spin qubits before and fits well with industrial chip manufacturing. Bringing together material growth, quantum theory and measurement, the goal is scalable germanium MOSFET devices that host competitive spin qubits. We contribute the theory.

item.title: New EU project QuKiT: a qubit that ignores noise
item.description: Our group is part of QuKiT, a new project funded by the European Innovation Council (EIC) Pathfinder Challenge, which started with a kickoff meeting in Delft. It brings together several research disciplines, industry and EU platforms around a new kind of qubit, the Kitmon. The goal is a qubit that is immune to local sources of noise and still easy to control, so that useful quantum computing would need a few thousand qubits rather than a few million.

item.title: Blueprint for quantum computing using electrons on helium
item.description: A new qubit for electrons on liquid helium that combines their spin with their quantized vertical motion, with schemes for gates and readout.

item.title: Professor at the University of Augsburg
item.description:
Since April 2023 I am professor for Quantum Information and Quantum Computing at the University of Augsburg, where I had already been an interim professor in 2021. With the Emmy Noether programme of the German Research Foundation (DFG) I am building up a junior research group here.

The university introduced its newly appointed professors, me among them: Neu nach Augsburg berufen (in German).

item.title: Open positions
item.description:
From April 2023 I will be a professor at the University of Augsburg and I am inviting motivated scientists to join our group to work on Quantum information theory based on solid state spin qubits. We have two PhD positions and two postdoc positions.

PhD positions: Theoretical modeling and simulation of spin qubits in quantum dots. Send your CV, letter of motivation, and the name and contact data from a possible reference by email. Feel free to contact me for further information!

item.title: An electron bus for nuclear spin entanglement
item.description:
Our article has been published in Physical Review Applied and highlighted as Editors’ Suggestion.

Entangled states of matter are a crucial resource for many quantum tasks, but producing such states deterministically between noninteracting parties is quite challenging, especially in solid-state systems. Here researchers offer a protocol to entangle two ensembles of nuclear spins that surround two quantum dots connected by an electron waveguide, employing sequential interaction of the nuclei with spin-polarized electrons. The authors numerically demonstrate the efficacy of the protocol, even in disordered and noisy setups, which suggests its feasibility with state-of-the-art techniques in quantum information processing.

item.title: Entangling Nuclear Spins in Distant Quantum Dots via an Electron Bus
item.description: Protocol for the deterministic generation of entanglement between two ensembles of nuclear spins surrounding two distant quantum dots.

item.title: Hole-spin qubits in Ge nanowire quantum dots: Interplay of orbital magnetic field, strain, and growth direction
item.description: How orbital magnetic effects, strain and growth direction shape hole-spin qubits in germanium nanowires, and which designs make the most of their spin-orbit interaction.

item.title: Emmy Noether group: a spin-based Floquet quantum processor
item.description:
The German Research Foundation (DFG) will fund my Emmy Noether junior research group Spin-based Floquet quantum information processor.

Spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots are a promising route to large quantum computers, but they still suffer from charge noise and only interact with their nearest neighbours. The idea of the project is to put time to work: qubits driven periodically in time (Floquet engineering) can be placed where noise hardly reaches them, switched on and off for long-distance couplings, used to probe the noise itself, and even organised into time crystals that keep their order while computing.

item.title: Squeezed hole spin qubits in Ge quantum dots with ultrafast gates at low power
item.description: Squeezing germanium quantum dots in one direction boosts the spin-orbit interaction by orders of magnitude, for ultrafast hole-spin gates at low power.

item.title: QSIT INSPIRE Postdoc Award
item.description:
I was awarded the INSPIRE award for postdocs launched by the National Center of Competence in Research Quantum Science and Technology.

The award supports excellent women for a postdoc project in a group of the QSIT network; mine is with Jelena Klinovaja and Daniel Loss in Basel. See the list of awardees (archived copy; the NCCR QSIT has ended and its website is offline).

item.title: Programable two-qubit gates in capacitively coupled flopping-mode spin qubits
item.description: A versatile set of two-qubit gates between neighbouring flopping-mode spin qubits within one node of a spin quantum computer.

item.title: Hybrid superconductor-semiconductor systems for quantum technology
item.description: A perspective on devices that combine superconducting circuits with semiconductor spin qubits: progress, limits and where the field is heading.

item.title: Flopping-mode electric dipole spin resonance
item.description: The flopping-mode configuration enables low-power spin control in quantum dot arrays.

item.title: Electric-field control and noise protection of the flopping-mode spin qubit
item.description: The flopping-mode spin qubit can be efficiently controlled and protected from charge fluctuations.

item.title: Optimized cavity-mediated dispersive two-qubit gates between spin qubits
item.description: Long-distance two-qubit gates between spin qubits, mediated by virtual photons in a superconducting cavity, and how to optimise their fidelity.

item.title: A coherent spin–photon interface in silicon
item.description: First demonstration of strong coupling between a single spin in silicon and a single microwave-frequency photon.

item.title: Input-output theory for spin-photon coupling in Si double quantum dots
item.description: Theory showing that a single electron spin in a silicon double quantum dot can couple strongly to a microwave photon, the route to a fully connected spin processor.

item.title: Random-walk topological transition revealed via electron counting
item.description: A classical random walk can be topological too, and the statistics of electron counting reveal it.

item.title: Topologically Enforced Bifurcations in Superconducting Circuits
item.description: A nonlinear topological insulator in superconducting circuits, whose topology shows up as bifurcations and chaos.

item.title: Full-counting statistics of time-dependent conductors
item.description: An efficient method for the full counting statistics of transport through conductors with arbitrary time dependence.

item.title: Transport, shot noise, and topology in AC-driven dimer arrays
item.description: In an ac-driven quantum dot chain, the current and its shot noise map out the topological phase diagram.

item.title: Dissipative long-range entanglement generation between electronic spins
item.description: A scheme that creates entanglement between two distant spin qubits in quantum dots and keeps it stable through dissipation.

item.title: Topological Instabilities in ac-Driven Bosonic Systems
item.description: AC driving can make bosonic modes unstable right at the edges of a system, protected by topology.

item.title: Edge-state blockade of transport in quantum dot arrays
item.description: A new transport blockade in quantum dot arrays and molecules, caused by Coulomb repulsion together with topological edge states.

item.title: Degenerate parametric oscillation in quantum membrane optomechanics
item.description: Optomechanical setups can realise degenerate parametric oscillation, a paradigm of dissipative phase transitions that optical cavities never could.

item.title: Floquet Majorana fermions in superconducting quantum dots
item.description: Periodically driven gates create Floquet Majorana modes in quantum dots coupled to superconductors, even where the undriven system has none.

item.title: Floquet engineering of long-range p-wave superconductivity
item.description: Periodic driving of the Kitaev chain creates topological phases with Floquet Majorana modes that the ac fields can tune and manipulate.

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.description:
This is the personal website of Mónica Benito. You can reach me at monica.benito@uni-a.de.

What this website collects

This website sets no cookies, uses no analytics or tracking, and loads nothing from other servers (no external fonts, videos or social media buttons).

When you open a page, the web server automatically records technical access data: your IP address, the date and time, the page requested, and the browser identification your browser sends. This is needed to deliver the website and to detect and block attacks. These logs are deleted after 14 days and are not combined with other data. The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in running the website securely).
